analysis.one_liner: Ends the antitrust exemption that lets ocean shipping lines fix prices together.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to strip ocean shipping lines of their price-fixing immunity was referred to the Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Ocean shipping lines that band together in 'conferences' can legally agree on freight rates because a 1984 law exempts them from the antitrust rules that forbid price-fixing in every other industry. This bill would amend the Sherman Act to end that exemption starting January 1, 1994, making colluding on shipping prices as illegal for ocean carriers as it is for anyone else. The bill was introduced by Senator Metzenbaum with four Republican cosponsors and sent to the Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: American importers, exporters, and small shippers who pay freight rates set by shipping conferences would gain leverage and likely pay less once rates had to be set competitively rather than by carrier cartels. Lower shipping costs would also flow into the prices of goods American consumers buy. Enforcement would be handled through the ordinary antitrust laws.

how_it_helps.text: Terminates, effective January 1, 1994, the Shipping Act of 1984's exemption from the antitrust laws insofar as it applies to ocean common carriers.

Adds a new section 9 to the Sherman Act defining ocean common carriers by reference to the Shipping Act of 1984 and ending their immunity, so carrier agreements on rates would face the same competition rules as other industries.

analysis.who_pays: Ocean shipping lines, especially those operating in conferences, would lose the legal ability to agree on common freight rates and surcharges, and could face antitrust lawsuits for collective pricing they currently conduct lawfully. Some carriers argue competitive rate-setting could make service less predictable and rates more volatile.

drawbacks.text: Ending the exemption removes a regime under which conferences published rates openly and were subject to Federal Maritime Commission oversight under the Shipping Act of 1984; the bill does not create a replacement regulatory framework, so rate-making would shift entirely to antitrust enforcement and the courts.

Carriers have long argued that conference agreements stabilize service and rates on routes where a few carriers operate; exposing them to antitrust liability could reduce cooperation on schedules and capacity, which shippers who value predictability might experience as disruption.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill takes a simple, low-cost approach: rather than build a new regulatory system, it subjects one industry to the same antitrust rules everyone else follows. The main design weakness is that it repeals the exemption without any transition or replacement oversight mechanism, so disputes would be resolved through litigation instead. That is a real but modest drawback weighed against ending an industry-wide exception to competition law.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 103rd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Metzenbaum introduced S. 1602 on October 29, 1993, with introductory remarks on the Senate floor.
Four Republican senators cosponsored the bill.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary on October 29, 1993.
No further action appears in the bill's history: no hearing, no committee report, no floor vote, before the Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ocean shipping conferences are better off, because they kept their exemption from antitrust law and continued setting rates collectively. American shippers and consumers are worse off, since a bill with bipartisan sponsorship never got a hearing or a vote.

for.name: Sen. Howard Metzenbaum
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-OH), bill sponsor and senior member of the Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction under Chairman Joseph Biden (D-DE)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or report — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Ocean shipping conferences
against.role: Carrier alliances that set collective freight rates under the Shipping Act of 1984
against.what_they_did: The conference industry opposed legislation to end the antitrust exemption, which would have made their collective rate-setting actionable under antitrust law.

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat sponsored the bill and all four of its cosponsors were Republicans, giving it bipartisan sponsorship before it stalled in committee.

industries.note: The bill would end the carriers' exemption from antitrust law, making their conference agreements on rates and surcharges subject to the Sherman Act. Their ability to set freight prices collectively is a cost embedded in the price of goods American businesses ship and consumers buy.

Businesses that move goods by sea would gain the ability to challenge collectively set freight rates, and smaller shippers would benefit most from competitive pricing. Exporters of American farm and manufactured goods pay these rates directly.

The Shipping Act regime the bill repeals had given the FMC a supervisory role over conference agreements; ending the exemption would shift oversight from agency review to antitrust enforcement, reducing the agency's role.
